newsitem.title: UK: New UK Tory boss confirms party shift to right.
newsitem.headline: New UK Tory boss confirms party shift to right.

text.p: William Hague, the new leader of Britain's crushed opposition Conservatives, on Saturday underlined his party's shift to the right by naming more hardliners to key shadow cabinet posts.
Hague appointed former party chairman Dr Brian Mawhinney as shadow home secretary and arch anti-European Iain Duncan-Smith to the post of shadow social security secretary.
David Heathcoat-Amory, who resigned from the previous government last year over his opposition to the proposed European single currency, becomes shadow chief secretary to the treasury.

The return of Mawhinney to the political limelight came as a surprise, for he was widely accused of running an ineffective campaign in the run-up to the May 1 rout which put Labour into power with a huge majority.

Another old-timer back in the fray is former party chairman Sir Norman Fowler, believed to have pulled out of frontline politics, who becomes shadow spokesman for environment, transport and the regions.

Although Hague did give some posts to moderate members of the party there is no doubt that the opponents of further integration with the European Union are in charge. Splits over policy towards the EU helped sink the party on May 1.
Hague announced the completion of the cabinet shortly after arriving in Scotland, which for the first time in history did not return a single Conservative member of parliament.
The prematurely balding 36-year-old, the youngest leader of his party for more than 200 years, is due to have a series of meetings with local officials to discuss how to revive the party's fortunes.

"We have many problems in our party and we're all aware of that...well now we have to fight back. We're going to fight back and I'm going to lead that fightback," Hague told reporters at Glasgow railway station.
On Thursday he stunned observers by naming Lord Cecil Parkinson, 65, a close ally of former prime minister Margaret Thatcher, to be party chairman for the next two years.
Hague won Thatcher's blessing in the leadership race and the "Iron Lady" confirmed her support by attending his victory party on Thursday night.

He also gave key posts to three of his right wing rivals in the leadership election and must have been happy that right-winger John Redwood -- a consistent Hague critic -- decided to rejoin the fold by taking the job of shadow trade and industry secretary.

But there was no job for Kenneth Clarke, the pro-European former Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister), who had made clear he would not serve on the opposition front benches unless he won the leadership.

Hague made clear that one of the main Conservative rallying calls in Scotland would be opposition to Labour's plans for a referendum on whether to set up a regional parliament with limited right to set its own tax.
Labour says devolution will satisfy Scotland's desire to have more say over its own affairs while opponents say it could help break up the country.
"I certainly fear it would lead to great disillusionment and bitterness in the long run," Hague told reporters.
